course.title: Acute appendicitis
course.html:
= acute inflammation of vermiform appendix; most common abdominal surgical emergency

Anatomy

  • Located in right iliac fossa
  • Length 6-12cm
  • 2 cm beneath ileocecal valve
  • Mesoappendix = mesentery that connects terminal ileum with appendix
  • Arterial blood supply - appendicular artery - ileocolic artery - superior mesenteric artery
  • Venous circulation goes to superior mesenteric vein
  • Appendix has immunological function through immunoglobuline secretion (lymphoid follicles)
    • number increases during puberty and declines 20-30 years

gradually

Etiology

  • Peak incidence 10 - 30/40 years, decreases with age
  • Coprolites and lymphoid tissue hyperplasia = most frequent causes
  • Less common: parasites, fruit & vegetable seeds, strictures and tumors
  • Luminal obstruction + continuous secretion of appendiceal mucosa + bacterial multiplication
  • increased intraluminal pressure
    • distention of appendix → pain in lower abdomen
    • interrruption of venous and lymphatic flow → parietal edema, hyperemia and microbial penetration into mucosa
Catarrhal appendicitis- Initial, limited to mucosa and submucosa
Phlegmonous appendicitis- Inflammatory process spreads to serosa of appendix and parietal peritoneum
→ localized pain at right iliac fossa
- If it progresses further → enlarged, congested, frail appendix; covered with
false membranes & purulent fluid
- Mesoappendix congested and thickened
Gangrenous appendicitis- Gradual distension and local circulatory dysfunction → venous and arterial
thrombosis → ischemic lesions with necrotic areas
- Appendix becomes flaccid, dark-red with black necrotic areas, edema of
mesentery and intraperitoneal pus
- Perforation occurs → development of appendicular block, appendicular
abscess or diffuse peritonitis

Clinical

  • Abdominal pain (sudden or progressive)
    • Initially epigastric or periumbilical; later after 4-6 h at right iliac fossa; intensified with effort
    • Depending on location of appendix
PeriumbilicallyRetro-ileal position
Right flankRetro-cecal position
Right hypochondriumSub-hepatic position
PelvisPelvic position
  • Anorexia (constant and early symptom)
  • Nausea, vomiting (rare)
  • Fever (around 38°C)
  • Transit disorders (mainly constipation, rarely diarrhea)

Physical exam

  • Tenderness in right iliac fossa = cardinal sign
McBurney pointPain, definitive for acute appendicitis
(outer 1/3 on a line drawn from umbilicus to right anterior superior iliac spine)
Blumberg signPain during sudden decompression, irritation of parietal peritoneum, always means diffuse
peritonitis if present
Grassmann MendelPain in right iliac fossa on percussion, also only present in diffuse peritonitis
sign or Bell sign
GuardingGuardingVoluntary - due to painful palpation, which can be conscious eliminated
Involuntary - abdominal spasm caused by peritoneal inflammation, cannot be suppressed
Rovsing signPalpation of left lower abdominal quadrant increases pain in right lower quadrant
Psoas signPsoas signAbdominal pain felt by passively extending thigh of patient lying on his side with knees
extended or flex thigh at hip
Positive in retrocaecal position → irritates iliopsoas muscle
Antalgic positionPatient in right lateral decubitus, avoids any movement, maintains flexion of right thigh
CutaneousMay be first clinical sign
hyperesthesia

Specific characteristics related to age

Infants and children- Difficult due to inability to properly communicate and multiple other gastrointestinal
childhood disorders
- Diagnosis is belated till after perforation occurs → evolution to generalized peritonitis is
fast, due to inability of underdeveloped omentum to block perforation
Elderly- Present milder symptoms, fever and leukocytosis only slightly increased, pain is mild or
even absent
- Atypical clinical picture, belated diagnosis and rapid evolution towards perforation
→ increased morbidity and mortality
Pregnant women- Difficult → enlarged uterus causes displacement of appendix → alters location of pain,
leukocytosis is physiological during pregnancy
- Many symptoms are non-specific

Diagnostics

  • Leukocytosis (10-18 000), high PMN´s → > 18 000 suggests perforation with/ without abscess; normal values don´t

exclude diagnosis

  • Urine analysis → DD with kidney diseases
  • Plain abdominal X-ray → signs of perforation and DD for kidney stones
  • Abdominal US → thickening of appendiceal wall and peri-cecal fluid accumulation; DD genital and urinary tract
  • Abdominal CT → useful in atypical clinical picture, when ultrasound fails to visualize changes, peri-appendiceal

abscess, DD genital and urinary tract

  • Laparoscopy → allows intra-abdominal evaluation + can be used as therapeutic method

Complications

Appendicular plastron
= appendicular block		- When surrounding organs adhere to appendix (cecum, ileum, omentum); secured by
peritoneal exudate rich in fibrin
- Usually occurs 3 days after onset of symptoms
- Regresses after antibiotic therapy and drainage, after 6 weeks it is completely healed
and appendectomy can be practiced
- May develop into an abscess or generalized peritonitis
Appendiceal abscess- Formed by transforming appendicular block into purulent collection
- Requires antibiotic treatment
- When abscess is large → percutaneous/ surgical drainage
- After 6 weeks, appendectomy can be performed
- Abscess may form fistula in hollow organ (bladder, small intestine), skin or
peritoneum (→ Peritonitis)
Generalized/ diffuse
peritonitis		- Direct perforation of appendix (necrosis)
- Formation of appendicular block → abscess → perforation into peritoneal cavity
→ generalized peritonitis
Treatment: appendectomy, rigorous lavage, drainage and antibiotic therapy

DD

Infants and children- Mesenteric lymphadenitis
- Acute gastroenteritis
- Intussusception (invagination)
- Meckel diverticulum
Adults- Renal or ureteric colic
- Perforated peptic ulcer
- Acute gastroenteritis
- Testicular torsion
- Pelvic inflammatory disease (adnexitis)
- Ruptured follicular cyst
- Torsioned ovarian cyst
- Ectopic pregnancy
- Acute cholecystitis
- Acute pancreatitis
Elderly- Cecum cancer
- Intestinal occlusion
- Entero-mesenteric infarction
-Testicular torsion
- Pelvic inflammatory disease (adnexitis)
- Ruptured follicular cyst
- Torsioned ovarian cyst
- Ectopic pregnancy

Treatment

  • Surgical emergency
Classical- Performed through oblique incision in right iliac fossa (McBurney incision)
LaparoscopicLaparoscopic- Uses at least 3 trocars
- Nowadays commonly performed

Main operative steps

  • Intraperitoneal examination
  • Identifying cecum and appendix
  • Freeing appendix and deliver it into wound
  • Ligation and transection of mesoappendix containing appendicular vessels
  • Ligation and transection at base of appendix → removing of appendix
  • Closing of abdominal wall wound

Medical treatment targets appendicular block, abscess, generalized peritonitis

  • Antibiotic therapy, symptomatic treatment (anti-inflammatory, antispasmodic and painkiller)

Post-OP complications

  • 1. Wound infection = most frequent post-operative complication
  • 2. Postoperative bleeding = often caused by slipping of ligature from mesoappendix (contains appendicular artery)
  • 3. Acute generalized or localized peritonitis through slipping of ligature from stump of appendix
  • 4. Intestinal obstruction through formation of post-operative adhesions
  • 5. Cardiac and pulmonary complications → DVT, pulmonary embolism = more frequent in elderly patients

book.html:
Acute appendicitis

Alin Fetti

DEFINITION

Acute appendicitis represents theacute inflammationof the vermiform appendixandis the most commonabdominalsurgical emergency.

ANATOMY

The appendix isan organthat has a tubularstructurewith a lengthof 612cm, the base of the appendix is located 2 cm beneath the ileocecal valve, at the junction of the three teniae. The mesoappendix is the part of the mesentery that connects the terminal ileum with the appendix.

The appendix is located along with the cecum in the right iliac fossa. The arterial blood supply is provided by the appendicular artery, which descends from theileocolic artery, branch of the superior mesenteric artery. The venous circulation is tributary to thesuperior mesenteric vein,and the lymphatic one to the lymph nodes situated at this level.

The appendix has an immunological function through the immunoglobuline secretion ofthe lymphoid follicles contained in the submucosal layer. The number of lymphoid follicles increases during puberty, remains constant for the next decade, in order to subsequently decline gradually with age.

EPIDEMIOLOGY:

The disease is rare atearly age, has a peak incidence between 10-40 years and its frequency decreases with age. Gender distribution shows a slight predominance of males.

Etiology and pathology

The luminal obstruction and the subsequent onset of bacterial infectionis the main cause of acute appendicitis,coprolites and lymphoid tissue hyperplasia are the most frequent causes of the obstruction. Other less common causes of obstruction are parasites, fruit and vegetable seeds, strictures and tumors.

Due to the luminal obstruction and continuoussecretion of appendiceal mucosa, increased intraluminal pressure occurs, determining the distention of the appendix, which causes vague and diffuse pain in the lower part of the abdomen.

The process of acute distension continues, due to the constant secretion of the apendicular mucosa and rapid multiplication of local appendiceal bacteria, which causes interrruption of venous and lymphatic flow, determining parietal edema, hyperemia andmicrobial penetration into mucosa. This initial chain of events leads to the constituition of the pathological form designated as catarrhal appendicitis.

The inflammatory processspreads to the serosaof the appendix and to theparietalperitoneumlocalizing the pain at the level ofthe right iliacfossa

If these lesions progress further,they determine phlegmonous appendicitis,characterized byan enlarged, congested , frail appendix , covered withfalsemembranes and purulent fluid on the serosal surface. Additionally themesoappendix is alsocongestedandthickened.

The gradual distension and local circulatory disfunction represented by venous and arterial thrombosis determines ischemic lesions,with the development of necrotic areas, a condition that is designated as gangrenous appedicitis. The appendixbecomesflaccid, dark-red with black necrotic areas,edema of themesenteryand intraperitonealpus. Upon this pathological backgroundperforationoccurs, which is followed by the development of an appendicular block, appendicular abscessordiffuse peritonitis.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS:

Abdominal pain is the major symptom of acute appendicitis. The onset of pain is sudden or progressive, initially located in the epigastric or periumbilical region, and later, after a period of 4-6 hours, moves slowly to the right iliac fossa. The pain is progressive and intesifies with effort. Depending on the location of the appendix the pain can be located periumbilically (retroileal position), in the right flank (retrocecal position) , right hipocondrum (subhepatic position) or in the pelvis (pelvic position).

Anorexia is a constant and early symptom.

Nausea and vomiting: vomiting is not frequent or lasting, usually appear one or two such episodes.

A fever of around 38 0C is present, exceeding this value represents a sign of perforation.

Transit disorders are represented by constipation andless often diarrhea.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Tenderness in the right iliac fossa is the cardinal sign on physical exam. McBurney's point is one of the painful areas considered definitive for acute appendicitis. It is defined as a point that lies one-third of distance laterally on a line drawn from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine.

Blumberg's sign: pain experienced duringsudden decompression afterprogressive application of pressure to the iliac fossa, expresses irritation of the parietal peritoneum.

Grassmann Mendel’s sign ( bell sign ): pain in the right iliac fossa onpercussion, expresses parietal peritoneum participation in the inflammatory process.

Voluntary guarding represents the voluntary spasm of the abdominal wall muscles due to painful palpation, which can be conscious eliminated.

Involuntary guarding represent involuntary abdominal spasm caused by peritoneal inflammation which cannot be willfully suppressed.

Rovsing’s sign: palpation of the left lower abdominal quadrant increases the pain felt in the right lower quadrant.

Psoas sign: abdominal pain felt by passively extending the thigh of a patient lying on his side with knees extended, or asking the patient to actively flex his thigh at the hip. The sign is positive when the inflamed appendix is in a retrocaecal position and irritates the iliopsoas muscle.

Cutaneous hyperesthesia accompanies the clinical picture of appendicitis and may be the first positive sign.

Antalgic position: patient in right lateral decubitus avoids any movement and maintains flexion of the right thigh on the abdomen.

Acute appendicitis has certain specific characteristics related to age:

In infants and children the diagnosis of acute appendicitis is difficult, due to the inability to obtain information from the patient and due to the multiple gastrointestinal childhood disorders. The diagnosis is belated, after perforation occurs and the evolution to generalized peritonitis is fast,due to the inability of the underdeveloped omentum to block the perforation.

In the elderly, appendicitis presents milder signs and symptoms, fever and leukocytosis are slightly increased and the pain is mild or even absent. The atypical clinical picture, belated diagnosis and the rapid evolution towards perforation causes increased morbidity and mortality in this age group.

Acute appendicitis in pregnant womenis the most common condition requiring surgery, excluding medical condition related to pregnancy. Diagnosis is difficult because many of the debut symptoms are nonspecific and are related to pregnancy, the enlarged uterus causes displacement of the appendix and alters location of the pain, leukocytosis is physiological during pregnancy.

COMPLEMENTARY EXPLORATIONS:

Leukocytosis reaches values between 10,000 to 18,000 / mm3, in relation with an increase in the polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Leukocytosis over 18,000 / mm3 suggests appendicular perforation with or without abscess formation. Normal values do not exclude the existence of an acute appendicitis.

Urine analysis is normal but it helps making the differential diagnosis with kidney diseases.

Plain abdominal radiography is useful only for differential diagnosis, it can rarely distinguish a coprolite.

Abdominal ultrasound reveals thickening of the appendiceal wall and pericecal fluid accumulation. It is also useful for the diagnosis of appendicular plastron and in the differential diagnosis of genital and urinary tract disorders.

Abdominal CT is useful in case of an atypical clinical picture and when ultrasound fails to visualize the pathological changes in the appendix, for diagnosis ofperiappendicealabscess formation and differential diagnosis of genital and urinary tract disorders.

Laparoscopy allows intra-abdominal exploration for diagnostic purpose and can be used as a therapeutic method.

EVOLUTION AND COMPLICATIONS:

The appendicular plastron (appendicular block) occurs when the surrounding organs (cecum, ileum, omentum) adhere to the inflamed appendix, forming a conglomerate secured by a peritoneal exudate rich in fibrin. The appendicular block usually occurs 3 days after the onset of the symptoms. It regresses under adequate antibiotic therapy and after a period of 6 weeks it is completely healed and appendectomy can be practiced. In certain cases, the appendicular plastron may develop into an abscess or generalized peritonitis. Classically, conservative treatment is recommended in a appendicular block, but an experienced surgeon can usually practice appendectomy. If the block is too compact, a drainage must be at least performed.

Appendiceal abscess is formed by transforming the appendicular block into a purulent collection. It requires antibiotic treatment, and when the abscess is large, percutaneous drainage or surgical drainage must be associated. After a period of 6 weeks it is desirable to carry out the appendectomy. The abscess may develop a fistula,an abnormal connection, that opens at the skin surface or into a hollow organ (bladder, small intestine) or into the peritoneum, causing generalized peritonitis.

Diffuse peritonitis.

In the absence of treatment, acute appendicitis can have a rapid and unfavorable evolution to perforation, determining generalized peritonitis.

Diffuse peritonitis can also develop following the sequence: onset of acute appendicitis - apparent regression -perforation and generalized peritonitis.

Diffuse peritonitis can also developfollowing the nextsteps: acute appendicitis- formation of an appendicular block followed by abcess formation – abscess perforation in the peritoneal cavity, determining generalized peritonitis.

The treatment of generalized peritonitis consists of appendectomy, rigorous lavage of the peritoneal cavity, drainage and antibiotic therapy.

DIFFERENTIALS

In children: mesenteric lymphadenitis, acute gastroenteritis, intussusception, Meckel diverticulum.

Adults: renal or ureteric colic, perforated peptic ulcer, acute gastroenteritis, testicular torsion, pelvic inflammatory disease (adnexitis), ruptured follicular cyst, torsioned ovarian cyst, ectopic pregnancy, acute cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis.

In the elderly: cecum cancer, intestinal occlusion, entero-mesenteric infarction.

TREATMENT:

The treatment of acute appendicitis is surgical and can be performed using either classical or laparoscopic techniques.

Classic appendectomy is performed through an oblique incision in the right iliac fossa (McBurney incision). The laparoscopic approach uses at least three trocars.

The main operative steps are: intraperitoneal examination, identifying the cecum and the appendix, freeing the appendix and deliver it into the wound,ligation and transection of the mesoappendix containing the apendicular vessels,ligation and transectionat the base of the appendix, removing of the appendix, closing of the abdominal wall wound.

Medical treatment targets the appendicular block and accompanies surgery in appendiceal abscess and generalized peritonitis. It is represented by antibiotic therapy, symptomatic treatment - anti-inflammatory, antispasmodic and painkiller.

POSTOPERATIVE COMPLICATIONS:

Wound infection is the most frequentpostoperative complication.

Postoperative bleeding is often caused by slipping of the ligature from the mezoappendix (that contains the appendicular artery) .

Acute generalized or localized peritonitis occurs through slipping of the ligature from the stump of the appendix .

Intestinalobstructionoccursthrough the formation ofpostoperative adhesions.

Cardiac and pulmonary complications,deep vein thrombosisandpulmonary embolismoccurmore frequentlyin elderly patients.

PROGNOSISIn acuteappendicitis, afavorableprognosisdepends ona correct and earlydiagnosis.
